title: You Asked God for Purpose. He Gave You People to Love, Work to Do, and Obedience You Called “Too Ordinary.”
paragraphs: You Asked God for Purpose. He Gave You People to Love, Work to Do, and Obedience You Called “Too Ordinary.”
Maybe you haven't missed your calling. Maybe you've been standing inside it while waiting for something more impressive to arrive.
You prayed for purpose.
You asked God to show you why you're here.

You watched testimonies of people who seemed to have discovered the thing they were born to do. Someone launched a ministry. Someone wrote the book. Someone moved across the world. Someone built the business. Someone stood beneath stage lights and told thousands of people how God called them.
And somewhere between their breakthrough and your ordinary Tuesday morning, a quiet fear began growing inside you.
What if I'm wasting my life?
Because your life doesn't feel spectacular.
You wake up.
You make the coffee.
You answer messages.
You go to work.
You study.
You wash dishes.
You care for children or aging parents.
You sit in traffic.
You pay bills.
You help somebody who may never thank you.
You fight temptations nobody knows you're fighting.
You forgive someone who doesn't realize how deeply they wounded you.
You pray when you don't feel anything.
You open your Bible when heaven seems silent.
You show up again.
And again.
And again.
And because none of it looks dramatic enough to become a testimony video, you quietly wonder whether any of it matters.
But what if the problem isn't that God hasn't given you purpose?
What if He already has...
and you dismissed much of it because it looked too ordinary?
Paul writes:
Then only a few verses later:
“And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.”
— Colossians 3:17, 23–24
There is something almost unsettling about those words.
Paul doesn't say, “Whatever spectacular thing you eventually discover…”
He says:
Whatever you do.
The Greek is startlingly comprehensive.
πᾶν ὅ τι ἐὰν ποιῆτε
pan ho ti ean poiēte
In context, the thought is essentially: whatever you may do.
Not only preaching.
Not only missions.
Not only ministry platforms.
Not only the moments people applaud.
Whatever you do.
And then Paul says:
ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐργάζεσθε
ek psychēs ergazesthe
Literally carrying the sense of working “from the soul”—wholeheartedly, from the inner person.
Why?
τῷ κυρίῳ
for the Lord.
Then comes the line that changes the entire room:
τῷ κυρίῳ Χριστῷ δουλεύετε
tō Kyriō Christō douleuete.
You are serving the Lord Christ.
Read that slowly.
Because somebody desperately needs to hear it before another year disappears while they wait for their “real purpose” to begin.
You are serving Christ.
The context of Colossians 3 isn't a conference filled with celebrity Christians discovering their dreams.
Paul is speaking directly into households.
Marriage.
Parenting.
Family relationships.
Work.
Authority.
Responsibility.
Daily conduct.
The painfully ordinary architecture of human life.
And into that ordinary world, Paul places Jesus Christ at the center.
That means Christianity does something astonishing to ordinary life.
It makes the ordinary holy when the ordinary is surrendered to Christ.
You wanted God to give you a mission.
He gave you someone difficult to love.
You wanted Him to use you.
He gave you work requiring integrity when nobody was watching.
You wanted a platform.
He gave you a family.
You wanted influence.
He gave you one hurting friend who needed somebody to listen.
You wanted a spiritual breakthrough.
He showed you something you needed to repent of.
You wanted to change the world.
He asked you to change the way you speak to the people living in your house.
And you almost missed Him...
because obedience wasn't wearing stage lights.
There is a generation exhausted by the pressure to become extraordinary.
We have been taught to optimize ourselves, brand ourselves, discover ourselves, monetize ourselves, distinguish ourselves, and somehow construct lives impressive enough to prove that we existed.
Even purpose can become another form of anxiety.
What's my calling?
What's my destiny?
What's God's big plan for me?
Those aren't necessarily wrong questions.

God genuinely calls people into particular assignments. Scripture contains dramatic commissions. Moses had the burning bush. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up. Jeremiah was appointed to prophetic ministry. Paul encountered the risen Christ on the road to Damascus.
But here's what we conveniently forget.
Moses spent decades in obscurity before the burning bush.
David knew what it meant to tend sheep before wearing a crown.
Jesus Himself spent most of His earthly life outside the public ministry recorded in detail in the Gospels.
Think about that.
The eternal Son of God entered human history...
and for years there were no crowds following Him.
No feeding of five thousand.
No Sermon on the Mount.
No public miracles recorded from those hidden years.
There was ordinary human life in Nazareth.
Then, when His public ministry began, Jesus didn't spend His days chasing applause.
He touched people society avoided.
He welcomed children.
He ate with sinners.
He washed feet.
He stopped for people everyone else was walking past.
And ultimately, He obeyed the Father all the way to a Roman cross.
The world saw scandal.
Heaven was accomplishing redemption.
The cross itself should permanently destroy our assumption that God's greatest purposes must look impressive to human eyes.
To Rome, crucifixion was humiliation.
To spectators, Jesus looked defeated.
To His frightened disciples, everything appeared to be collapsing.
Yet through the very place that looked like shame, God was accomplishing salvation.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
The stone didn't get the final word.
Sin didn't get the final word.
Death didn't get the final word.
And your culture doesn't get the final word about what makes a life meaningful either.
Jesus does.
That is why the Gospel doesn't merely give you a better “purpose strategy.”
It gives you a new Lord.
This is where Christianity confronts the modern obsession with finding ourselves.
Biblical purpose begins not with, “What would make me feel significant?”
It begins with Jesus Christ.
We were made through Him and for Him.
We don't ultimately belong to ourselves.
And because sin separated us from God, our deepest problem was never that we hadn't discovered the perfect career, ministry niche, relationship, or dream.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed redemption.
We needed Jesus.
The Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
He carried what we could never carry.
At the cross, the sinless Savior gave Himself for the guilty.
And He rose victorious.
So repentance isn't abandoning your purpose.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One in whom your life finally finds its proper center.
Grace isn't God helping you become the impressive person you've always dreamed of becoming.
Grace is God rescuing you from sin and bringing you into life with Christ.
And once Jesus becomes Lord, ordinary things begin looking different.
That office isn't merely an office anymore.
That classroom isn't merely a classroom.
That kitchen isn't merely a kitchen.
That hospital room isn't merely a hospital room.
That construction site isn't merely a construction site.
That night shift isn't merely a night shift.
That conversation with your child isn't merely another interruption.
That opportunity to forgive isn't merely another inconvenience.
That temptation you resist when nobody sees isn't meaningless.
That apology you owe isn't beneath your calling.
That prayer whispered while washing dishes isn't wasted.
That lonely act of integrity nobody applauds isn't forgotten.
You can do these things for the Lord Christ.
This does not mean every job is good, every circumstance should remain unchanged, every ambition is wrong, or every opportunity should be ignored.
Scripture does not command passivity.
There may be doors God genuinely wants you to walk through.
There may be gifts you need to develop.
There may be injustices you should confront.
There may be careers you should leave, ministries you should begin, places you should go, risks you should take, and sacrifices obedience will require.
But never confuse bigger with more faithful.
Never confuse visibility with fruitfulness.
Never confuse applause with God's approval.
And never become so obsessed with tomorrow's assignment that you repeatedly disobey today's.
Maybe you have spent months asking:
“God, show me my purpose.”
And perhaps one answer has been sitting across the dinner table from you.
Love them.
Maybe the answer clocks in beside you every morning.
Serve faithfully.
Maybe the answer keeps appearing as the same conviction.
Repent.
Maybe it sounds like:
Forgive.
Tell the truth.
Keep your word.
Honor your spouse.
Raise your children in the Lord.
Care for your parents.
Help the weak.
Encourage the discouraged.
Give generously.
Pray secretly.
Resist temptation.
Make peace.
Do honest work.
Love your neighbor.
Share Christ.
Stay faithful.
None of that sounds glamorous.
That's precisely why we underestimate it.
We want a calling that makes us feel extraordinary.
Jesus often calls us into faithfulness that makes Him look extraordinary.
There is a difference.
And maybe that is what has been hurting you.
Maybe you've secretly been measuring your life by other people's highlight reels.
Someone younger than you is already successful.
Someone you went to school with seems miles ahead.
Someone's ministry exploded.
Someone bought the house.
Someone got married.
Someone had children.
Someone found their dream career.
Someone seems certain about everything you're still praying about.
Meanwhile you're sitting there thinking:
Lord... what about me?
And comparison begins whispering something cruel.
You're late.
You missed it.
God forgot you.
You're wasting your life.
But Scripture doesn't tell you to run somebody else's race.
Faithfulness cannot be measured by another person's timeline.
There are seasons when obedience looks like going.
There are seasons when obedience looks like staying.
There are seasons when faith produces visible fruit quickly.
There are seasons when you sow faithfully and see almost nothing.
There are seasons when God entrusts you with much.
There are seasons when your entire assignment seems to be surviving suffering without abandoning Christ.
And sometimes one of the holiest sentences a believer can say is:
“Jesus, I will obey You here.”
Here.
Not when the promotion arrives.
Here.
Not when everybody finally recognizes your gift.
Here.
Not when your following grows.
Here.
Not when you're married.
Here.
Not when you're financially comfortable.
Here.
Not when your mental picture of your future finally becomes reality.
Here.
Today.
With these people.
With these responsibilities.
With this opportunity to obey.
Because the question that may matter more than “What is God's spectacular purpose for my life?” is:
“How can I faithfully belong to Jesus in the life He has placed before me today?”
That question can change everything.
Suddenly, the mother changing another diaper can worship.
The father leaving early for another exhausting shift can worship.
The student refusing to cheat can worship.
The employee doing honest work without supervision can worship.
The teenager resisting hidden temptation can worship.
The caregiver washing an elderly parent's clothes can worship.
The Christian choosing gentleness during an argument can worship.
The believer quietly serving a church without recognition can worship.
The wounded person choosing forgiveness can worship.
The exhausted disciple whispering, “Jesus, help me stay faithful,” can worship.
Not because every mundane activity is automatically righteous.
But because life submitted to Christ can be lived in His name and for His glory.
And maybe this is the freedom you've been begging God for without realizing it.
You don't have to become famous to matter.
You don't have to become impressive to be faithful.
You don't have to manufacture a dramatic destiny before your life becomes useful to God.
Your greatest calling isn't becoming somebody strangers admire.
It is belonging to Jesus Christ.
And from that belonging comes obedience.
Sometimes enormous.
Sometimes costly.
Sometimes public.
Sometimes so ordinary that nobody except God knows what it cost you.
But He knows.
Colossians says:
“Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance.”
People may overlook your faithfulness.
Jesus doesn't.
People may never understand the sacrifice.
Jesus does.
People may never applaud the decision you made when compromise would have been easier.
Jesus saw it.
The world might never know your name.
Jesus does.
And if Jesus knows your name, why are you allowing strangers' recognition to determine whether your life matters?
There is another danger here, though.
We can read an article about ordinary faithfulness and turn even that into self-salvation.
I'll work harder.
I'll become more disciplined.
I'll prove myself faithful.
No.
Come back to the Gospel.
You are not saved because you performed ordinary obedience perfectly.
You haven't.
Neither have I.
We have wasted time.
Ignored people.
Chosen selfishness.
Neglected prayer.
Failed to love.
Compromised.
Complained.
Envied.
Compared.
Hidden sin.
Wanted recognition.
Sometimes we even wanted God's gifts more than God Himself.
That's the scandal.
And this is grace:
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
The Savior who calls you to faithfulness is the Savior who died for your unfaithfulness.
The hands commanding your surrender are scarred hands.
The voice calling you home belongs to the Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep.
Christian obedience isn't an attempt to purchase God's love.
It flows from grace.
We love because He first loved us.
We obey the One who redeemed us.
And when we fail, we don't run deeper into hiding.
We run back to Christ in repentance and faith.
That is the heartbeat of everything Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim:
Your failure doesn't have to become your final chapter.
Your wasted years don't have to have the last word.
Your hidden sin doesn't have to remain hidden.
Your confusion about purpose doesn't have to control another decade.
Jesus still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
And maybe your next chapter doesn't begin with discovering something spectacular.
Maybe it begins tomorrow morning.
The alarm rings.
Nobody applauds.
You get up.
You pray.
You open Scripture.
You love the people God has entrusted to you.
You do your work with integrity.
You refuse the temptation.
You apologize.
You forgive.
You encourage someone.
You tell somebody about Jesus.
You serve.
You endure.
You repent when you fail.
You return to Christ.
And then you wake up and do it again.
Not because you're trying to become worthy of God's grace.
Because grace found you.
Because Christ redeemed you.
Because Jesus is worthy.
And think about one person who desperately needs this truth.
Maybe it's the young adult panicking because everyone else seems ahead.
Maybe it's the friend who believes their ordinary job doesn't matter.
Maybe it's the mother who wonders whether anyone sees her sacrifice.
Maybe it's the father quietly carrying responsibilities nobody notices.
Maybe it's the believer waiting for a “big calling” while slowly becoming discouraged.
Send this to them.
You may never know how God uses one faithful share to put biblical encouragement in front of someone who desperately needed it.
Because comparison will probably come back.
The pressure to become impressive will probably come back.
And when it does, return to Colossians 3 and remember:
You serve the Lord Christ.

Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, never by financially supporting a ministry. But voluntary generosity can help sustain Gospel-centered work and allow more Scripture-based resources to keep reaching people.

Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite the struggling believer. Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening. Invite the seeker with questions. Even invite the unbelieving friend willing to hear what Christianity actually says about Jesus.
Give yourself to Christ.
Maybe you asked God for purpose...
and He gave you people to love.
Work to do.
Sin to repent of.
Someone to forgive.
Someone to encourage.
A responsibility to carry.
A Gospel to share.
A Savior to follow.
And an ordinary Tuesday in which to do it.
Perhaps your life isn't waiting to become meaningful.
Perhaps Jesus is waiting for your faithful yes right where you are.
The ordinary life you keep trying to escape may be the very altar where Jesus is teaching you how to become faithful.
